The two divergence equations constrain net outward ﬂux. The two curl equations constrain
circulation and couple spatial ﬁeld variation to time variation and current. They describe the
same electric and magnetic ﬁelds at the same positions and times.
It is useful to speak of induction, but the equations are not a sequence in which an electric
ﬁeld ﬁrst creates a magnetic ﬁeld from nothing, which then creates a new electric ﬁeld. A
physical solution must satisfy all four relations, the material model, the source speciﬁcation,
and appropriate initial and boundary conditions together.
Nonzero ﬁelds can exist in a
source-free region; ρ = 0 and J = 0 there do not mean that the ﬁelds or their curls vanish.
1.2.7
Time-harmonic ﬁelds and phasors
The changing ﬁeld now has a place in the laws, but writing out its full time dependence repeatedly
can obscure the comparison between readings. Change the drive to a sinusoidal source and consider
the periodic response after its transient has decayed. What repeats from cycle to cycle, and what
diﬀers from point to point? Phasors will let us keep those pieces separate. The same idea also
prepares us to read prescribed wave patterns; a single oscillating reading alone does not establish
how a wave propagates.
One oscillation, three pieces of information.
Imagine keeping a voltmeter at one location
and watching its reading rise, fall, change sign, and repeat. Three numbers describe a sinusoidal
reading: its largest magnitude, how long one repetition takes, and where in that repetition it
begins. These are the peak amplitude A, the period T, and the initial phase ϕ. The amplitude has
the units of the measured quantity; for a voltage it is in volts. The period is in seconds. Phase is
an angle specifying a position within a cycle: adding 2π radians, or 360◦, gives the same reading.

Frequency f = 1/T counts cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). Angular frequency ω = 2πf = 2π/T
counts radians per second. The accumulated phase at time t is therefore ωt + ϕ. A cosine begins
at its positive maximum when this angle is zero:
v(t) = A cos(ωt + ϕ),
A ≥0.
(1.28)
For two signals of the same frequency, increasing the phase by ∆ϕ > 0 shifts a corresponding cycle
feature earlier by ∆ϕ/ω. This is a phase lead; compare corresponding cycles because phase repeats
modulo 2π. It is not a larger amplitude or a larger frequency.
A time-harmonic quantity has one sinusoidal frequency.
In a linear, time-invariant system, a
general excitation can be decomposed into Fourier components, solved frequency by frequency,
and reconstructed by adding the responses. We ﬁrst learn to handle one such component.
Why introduce a complex arrow?
Draw an auxiliary plane with a horizontal real axis and a
vertical imaginary axis. These axes are bookkeeping axes, not two directions in physical space. A
point a + jb has horizontal coordinate a and vertical coordinate b, where j2 = −1. Multiplication
by j rotates an arrow in this plane by 90◦counterclockwise.

What a phasor contains
eV stores amplitude and initial phase; the associated frequency must be stated separately. It
has the same units as v(t). Here | eV | = A is a peak amplitude. The root-mean-square (RMS)
value, deﬁned as the square root of the mean of v2 over one cycle, is A/
√
2 for a sinusoid. No
RMS conversion is implicit in these notes.
Complex notation does not assert physical rotation of a voltage or of the electric-ﬁeld vec-
tor. Physical rotation would require a particular relationship between diﬀerent spatial ﬁeld
components; a single oscillating component need only change size and reverse sign.
Reading length and angle without losing the quadrant.
The same phasor can be given
by coordinates or by length and angle:
eV = a + jb = Aejϕ,

The notation atan2(b, a) means the angle of the point (a, b) measured from the positive real axis,
using both coordinate signs to choose its quadrant. It is not division by 2. For example, a negative
real part and positive imaginary part place the arrow in quadrant II. The simpler calculation
tan−1(b/a) cannot distinguish opposite quadrants by itself. Phase angles diﬀering by 360◦represent
the same phasor. A zero-amplitude phasor has no meaningful phase angle. Exponents use radians
unless a degree symbol is written.
Choose one sinusoidal reference
The convention throughout is a cosine obtained as the real part with e+jωt. Convert sine
signals before reading oﬀtheir phasors:
sin θ = cos(θ −90◦),
−sin θ = cos(θ + 90◦),
−cos θ = cos(θ + 180◦).
Thus a negative amplitude is absorbed into the phase, leaving A ≥0. Multiplication by j
adds 90◦; multiplication by −j subtracts 90◦. Changing the time convention to e−jωt would
change several signs, so conventions must not be mixed.

and the hats denote unit directions in physical space. At each point, the electric-ﬁeld vector has
three physical components in V/m. Each component can oscillate with its own amplitude and
initial phase. To describe a single frequency, assign a complex vector amplitude to each position:

The ﬁeld arrow at each position is parallel to the physical y-axis, because of ˆy: it points along +y
or −y according to the cosine sign. The phase changes when one moves along x, because of e−jβx.
There is no dependence on the coordinates y or z, so all points with the same x have the same
ﬁeld at the same instant. The expression describes a ﬁeld throughout three-dimensional space,
even though only one spatial coordinate is needed to specify its variation.
Two diﬀerent cuts through the same space–time function.
A time trace holds the position
ﬁxed and lets the clock run. A spatial snapshot holds the time ﬁxed and compares positions. Both
can look sinusoidal, but their horizontal axes have diﬀerent meanings and diﬀerent units. A plotted
curve of Ey against x is a graph of ﬁeld values; it is not a wavy path taken by a charge or a thin
physical strip containing the entire ﬁeld.

Write a representative scalar component as
g(x, t) = A cos ψ(x, t),

displacement by one wavelength λ changes phase by one full turn, so

Wave velocity and local oscillation velocity.
A mechanical string gives a helpful analogy,
provided we distinguish the motion of the pattern from the motion of the string. Let y(x, t) denote
transverse displacement, not an additional independent coordinate. For a right-moving pattern,
write y(x, t) = F(x −vpt), where F speciﬁes its shape.
A material point keeps its horizontal
coordinate x but moves up and down. Its vertical velocity is the partial derivative with respect to
time, meaning that x is held ﬁxed:
vy(x, t) = ∂y

The prime on F denotes the ordinary derivative of its one argument. For a right-moving wave, a
rising spatial slope means the point moves down; a falling slope means it moves up. A crest can
propagate even though the point momentarily at the crest has zero vertical velocity. A left-moving
pattern has the opposite sign. This rule concerns a graph of a mechanical displacement. For an
electromagnetic ﬁeld, the oscillating quantity is a ﬁeld value, and no string or material particle
needs to travel with it.

From one spatial coordinate to three: what does k · r mean?
A wave need not travel
parallel to the chosen x-, y-, or z-axis. To describe an arbitrary direction, collect the three spatial
phase rates into the wave vector k = kx ˆx + ky ˆy + kz ˆz. Its components have units rad/m. For the
time convention used here, deﬁne
ψ(r, t) = ωt −k · r + ϕ0,
k · r = kxx + kyy + kzz.
The dot denotes the scalar product, so k · r is one number, not another vector. It gives the spatial
angle appearing in the phase. At a ﬁxed time, a displacement ∆r changes phase by −k · ∆r. For
example, changing only x changes phase by −kx∆x.
To expose the geometry, deﬁne the magnitude k = |k| =
q
k2x + k2y + k2z > 0 and the unit propa-
gation direction ˆk = k/k. Now let s = ˆk · r be the signed projection distance of the position along
this direction. Then
k · r = ks,
ψ = ωt −ks + ϕ0.
(1.35)
This is exactly the one-dimensional phase formula with s in place of x. Moving sideways, perpen-
dicular to k, does not change s or the phase. At a ﬁxed time, the points with one given value of
s form an entire plane perpendicular to k. Such a constant-phase plane is called a phase front.
Consecutive planes with the same phase modulo 2π are separated by λ = 2π/k, measured along
ˆk.
These planes are not material walls. They mark locations whose ﬁeld oscillations are at the same
stage. As time increases, a plane of ﬁxed phase advances along +ˆk at speed vp = ω/k for this
convention. The associated phase-velocity vector is vp = (ω/k)ˆk. This statement describes motion
of phase; questions about power or energy transport belong to the later wave-propagation chapter.

The ﬁeld arrow has a diﬀerent direction from the wave vector.
For the simple vector
wave considered here, let E0 be a ﬁxed real amplitude vector. It speciﬁes the physical axis along
which the electric ﬁeld oscillates, and its length is the peak ﬁeld strength. Multiplication by a real
cosine changes that arrow’s length and can reverse its direction:
E(r, t) = E0 cos(ωt −k · r),
eE(r) = E0e−jk·r.
(1.36)
The two vectors answer diﬀerent questions: E0 describes the ﬁeld at a point, while k describes
how its phase is arranged across space and which way that pattern moves. The phase fronts extend
in two transverse directions even when a drawing shows only one row of ﬁeld arrows. This real-
amplitude example has a ﬁxed ﬁeld axis. More general complex vector amplitudes can put the
spatial components at diﬀerent phases; that extension is the subject of polarisation later in the
course.
Worked example 1.18
Separating the two directions
Let E0 = (−2, 2, 1) V m−1 and k = (1, 2, −2) rad m−1. First form the scalar phase contribution:
k · r = kxx + kyy + kzz.
If x, y, z denote the numerical values of coordinates measured in metres, this is written compactly
as x + 2y −2z radians. Thus
eE(x, y, z) = (−2ˆx + 2ˆy + ˆz)e−j(x+2y−2z) V m−1.
This familiar shorthand must not be read as putting a dimensional length in an exponential. The
coeﬃcients really are 1, 2, −2 rad/m, and each coeﬃcient multiplies its coordinate in metres.

Worked example 1.19
What the curl equations do and do not imply
The Gauss equations constrain which spatial ﬁeld conﬁgurations are allowed. The curl equations
describe their time evolution. We can check whether this evolution preserves a Gauss constraint
already satisﬁed initially. Take the divergence of Ampère–Maxwell’s equation. The divergence of
a curl is zero, so its left side vanishes. Use continuity on the right:
0 = ∇· J + ∂
∂t(∇· D)
= −∂ρ
∂t + ∂
∂t(∇· D).
Thus ∂t(∇· D −ρ) = 0. Similarly, the divergence of Faraday’s law gives ∂t(∇· B) = 0.
These statements preserve any initial Gauss constraints; they do not by themselves set an arbitrary
time-independent diﬀerence to zero. If the Gauss equations hold initially, they continue to hold.
For a purely harmonic component at ω ̸= 0, the equations become
jω(∇· f
D −eρ) = 0,

B = 0,
so both harmonic Gauss equations follow directly. The restriction to a nonzero frequency is essential
when dividing by jω.
